                                How to read the map

                                Sources. There is no single Pausanias-like description of Rome. The history of the buildings is given by Livy, Varro, Dionysius, Cicero, the Res Gestae of Augustus, Suetonius, Cassius Dio and the inscriptions; the 4th-century regionary catalogues, in turn, list what stood in each region.

                                Excavations. In the 16th–19th centuries the Forum was known as a stone quarry and under the name “Campo Vaccino” (cow pasture). Systematic excavation began after 1803; between 1898 and 1905 Giacomo Boni dug down to the Republican-era and Archaic layers (Lapis Niger, Spring of Juturna, Regia, Iron Age cemetery). Today the Parco archeologico del Colosseo conducts the research; in 2020 an underground shrine linked to the cult of Romulus was presented beneath the steps of the Curia.

                                Lanciani layer. Rodolfo Lanciani’s 1:1000 atlas Forma Urbis Romae (1893–1901) over the whole area of the map: plates 1–4, 6–11 and 13–46, fitted into a uniform grid (for details see the Sources). Ancient remains in black, the city of the time (around 1900) in red, aqueducts and sewers in blue. At the control points the deviation is 1–8 m.

                                The imperial forums come from plate 22. Here the difference is especially clear: Lanciani drew the Forum of Caesar before the excavations of the 1930s, in a conjectured position, about 35 m further southeast than the real one, while the Forum and Markets of Trajan already largely agree with the modern survey.

                                The map was made largely before Boni’s excavations, begun in 1898, so it shows clearly what has come to light since then: on the site of the Basilica Aemilia Lanciani could only write the legend “locus basilicae Aemiliae”, the Lacus Curtius, the Lapis Niger and the Iron Age cemetery are still missing, and he drew the Regia according to the pre-excavation hypothesis, as a smaller rectangle. He gives the Temple of Divus Iulius as a reconstruction ringed by columns, and he took the large hall behind the Temple of Castor to be the Temple of Augustus.

                                Excavation data (SITAR). About 4,200 excavated or reconstructed ancient units from the open archaeological database of the Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma: walls, building phases, drains, roads, houses. Only units whose dating begins in AD 640 or earlier, or that are undated, are shown; medieval, modern and present-day layers (such as 19th-century palaces and streets) and geological layers are left off the map. They appear according to the year slider, so that, for example, the six Archaic building phases of the Regia (625–510 BC), the four phases of the Temple of Castor or the two phases of the Forum of Caesar can be viewed one after another. Their color shows their character (red: place of worship, brown: residential building, blue: water, gray: road, tan: other); the dashed line is the excavators’ reconstruction. Clicking any of them, the information panel shows the identification, the dating, the investigation and the description in English; the original Italian text can be expanded.

                                Marble Plan fragments. Those fragments of the marble plan of the city made between AD 203 and 211 (Forma Urbis Severiana) whose location has been identified, fitted to their real position in SITAR: the yellow patches are the fragments, with the lines of the ancient drawing inside them. The inscriptions of the Basilica Iulia and the Basilica Ulpia can also be read on them.

                                Scale. The bar at the bottom left shows 50 m, 100 Roman feet (29.6 m) and one actus (120 feet, 35.5 m).

                                Layers and walks

                                • Temple dedication days. The “Dedication day (dies natalis)”, “Senate meetings” and some “Vowed” rows on the temple cards (32 temples) come from J. D. Muccigrosso’s Temples of the Classical World database (Drew University / Rome Research Group, github.com/Jmuccigr/temples), which cites among others Ziolkowski, Stamper, Blake and Platner–Ashby; where the identification of the temple is disputed (Largo Argentina A, C, D), the row says so. Used with the author’s permission under a share-alike (CC BY-SA) licence; the temple data on this map are likewise available under CC BY-SA 4.0.
                                • Aqueducts. Frontinus, De aquaeductu (AD 97) 1.4–23, on the construction, length and end points of the aqueducts; Historia Augusta, Alexander Severus 25 (Aqua Alexandrina). Course: SITAR (measured remains and archaeological reconstructions), OpenStreetMap (standing arches; courses tagged as “approximate” only as estimates, shown faint); where no measured section exists: Waters of Rome / Aquae Urbis Romae (K. W. Rinne, University of Virginia; after Ashby, Lanciani and Quilici), estimated courses faint and dotted, courses hypothetical even according to the source sparsely dashed. Where the Waters of Rome lines can be compared with a measured section, their median distance from it is 6–37 m. Water features (nymphaea and fountains, distribution tanks and cisterns, baths and latrines, mithraea, sewers, ports and ferries, bridges, naumachiae, water mills, the Tiber bank boundary stones): the Waters of Rome items before AD 640, 288 features; 13 structures that already have their own card on the map (e.g. the Pons Fabricius, the Barberini Mithraeum, the Sette Sale) are not repeated, and 7 outside the map area are left out. The Waters of Rome does not record how certain a location is, so the map gives its own class: archaeologically known if there is an ancient SITAR unit of the same kind within 30 m (27) or if the source says the remains were found there (39); conjectural if the source itself calls the location or identification conjectural, or marks it with a question mark (31); the rest (191) are locations according to the source that we could not check against independent data.
                                • The main roads from gate to gate. SITAR (measured stretches of the road paving and reconstructions, the location of the gates of the Servian Wall); outside the gates Itiner-e: P. de Soto, A. Pažout, T. Brughmans et al., Itiner-e: A high-resolution dataset of roads of the Roman Empire, Scientific Data 12 (2025) 1731; dataset: Itiner-e static version 2024, Zenodo, CC BY 4.0.
                                • Early Christian Rome. Liber Pontificalis (the lives of the popes, their foundations and donations); Jerome, De viris illustribus. Location of the churches and catacombs: the center of the present-day church or catacomb as mapped in OpenStreetMap, or SITAR.
                                • Walks. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities 3.68, 7.72; Cicero, In Catilinam 1–3, In Verrem 2.1, Pro Murena, Philippics 1–2, Ad Atticum 13.44, De haruspicum responso; Sallust, Catiline; Plutarch (Aemilius Paullus, Marcellus, Cicero, Cato the Younger, Caesar, Brutus); Suetonius (Divus Iulius, Augustus, Nero, Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasianus, Domitianus); Appian, Civil Wars 2; Cassius Dio 44, 51, 53–54, 56, 62, 69; Tacitus, Annales 1 and 15, Historiae 1, 3, 4; Augustus, Res Gestae; Josephus, Jewish War 7; Ovid, Amores 3.2; Propertius 2.31, 4.2; Juvenal 10; Martial, Liber spectaculorum 2; Pliny, Naturalis historia 33–36; Strabo 5.3.8; Livy 1.12; Tertullian, Apologeticum 33; Ammianus Marcellinus 14, 16, 17, 27; Symmachus, Relatio 3; Ambrose, Epistulae 18; Jerome, De viris illustribus 15; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.25; Liber Pontificalis; Procopius, Wars 3–8; the continuator of the chronicle of Marcellinus Comes; Historia Augusta, Hadrian 19. The text of the stops is the map author’s own summary and translation, not a published translation.
                                • Walks from novels. Henryk Sienkiewicz, Quo Vadis (1896); chapter numbers follow Jeremiah Curtin's English translation (Boston, 1896; Project Gutenberg #2853). Notes beyond the novel: Tacitus, Annales 13.32, 15.38–44; the apocryphal Acts of Peter 35 (the “Quo vadis” scene). Dezső Kosztolányi, Nero, a véres költő (Nero, the Bloody Poet, 1922); references are to chapter titles (MEK 03254, Hungarian text). Notes beyond the novel: Tacitus, Annales 12.66–69, 13.3, 13.15–17, 13.25, 13.45–46, 14.15, 15.51–64; Suetonius, Claudius 44, Nero 6, 22, 30–31, 33, 45, 48–50; Pliny the Elder, Nat. hist. 33.54, 36.102; Horace, Satirae 1.8; Martial 1.3. Nicholas Wiseman, Fabiola, or the Church of the Catacombs (1854); references give the part and chapter number (Project Gutenberg #62254). Notes beyond the novel: Liber Pontificalis (Pope Marcellus); Historia Augusta, Alexander Severus 26; Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 13. Colleen McCullough, The First Man in Rome (1990), Hungarian translation Róma első embere by Anna Dániel and others, Árkádia, Budapest 1991, vols. I–II; references give the volume and page of this edition. Notes beyond the novel: Sallust, Jugurthine War 35, 73, 86; Plutarch, Marius 12, 29; Appian, Civil Wars 1.28–32; Orosius 5.17; Cicero, De domo sua 102, De oratore 2.197–203; Suetonius, Divus Iulius 46.
                                • Inscriptions. Epigraphic Database Roma (EDR), EpiDoc files, version 12 (Sapienza Università di Roma – Università di Napoli L’Orientale – Università di Firenze – Università di Foggia; S. Panciera, G. Camodeca, G. A. Cecconi, S. Orlandi, L. Fabriani, S. Evangelisti), Zenodo 2026, 10.5281/zenodo.18468635, CC BY 4.0. The summary is our own: inscriptions found in Rome (findspot: Roma), type as classified by EDR, dating from the EDR “notBefore–notAfter” data, findspots and roads from keywords in the findspot descriptions (insc/calc.py).
                                • Occupations in the inscriptions. Data: EDR (see “Inscriptions”). The summary is our own: a search for 127 Latin occupational titles in the texts of the inscriptions, grouped into nine sectors; every hit checked by reading (excluded items: occ/excl.py); legal status from case-agreeing markers in the name belonging to the title; military inscriptions and second copies of repeated inscriptions excluded; addresses from the place given after the title (occ/lex.py, occ/calc.py). The standard study of the subject: Sandra R. Joshel, Work, Identity, and Legal Status at Rome. A Study of the Occupational Inscriptions, Norman–London 1992.
                                • Legal status and imperial names over time. Data: EDR (see “Inscriptions”). The summary is our own: a search for the markers and for eight imperial family names in the texts of the inscriptions, counted once per inscription, without the second copies of inscriptions repeated under several EDR numbers; the emperors’ own names and the names of legions, buildings and tribes filtered out (nm/calc.py). Regnal years follow the standard chronology.
                                • Age and family in the epitaphs. Data: EDR (see “Inscriptions”), the inscriptions from Rome classified as epitaphs. The summary is our own: age from the Roman numeral after “vixit annis” and “annorum”, length of marriage from the phrase “cum quo/qua vixit annis”, the terms from kinship and household words in the dative (age/calc.py). On the limits and results of the method: K. Hopkins, On the Probable Age Structure of the Roman Population, Population Studies 20 (1966); R. Duncan-Jones, Age-rounding, Illiteracy and Social Differentiation in the Roman Empire, Chiron 7 (1977); R. P. Saller – B. D. Shaw, Tombstones and Roman Family Relations in the Principate, Journal of Roman Studies 74 (1984).
                                • The size of tomb plots. Data: EDR (see “Inscriptions”). The summary is our own: the Roman numerals in the phrases “in fronte pedes … in agro pedes …” and “quoquoversus pedes …”, without fragmentary numerals; 1 Roman foot = 29.6 cm (plot/calc.py).
                                • Soldiers in the epitaphs of Rome. Data: EDR (see “Inscriptions”), the inscriptions from Rome classified as epitaphs. The summary is our own: a search for unit names in the text; age from the numeral after “vixit annis”, length of service from that after “militavit annis” and “stipendiorum”; origin from the ethnic name after “natione” (mil/calc.py).
                                • Christian inscriptions (3rd–8th century). Epigraphic Database Bari (EDB) – Inscriptions by Christians in Rome (3rd–8th cent. CE), EpiDoc files (C. Carletti, A. E. Felle, A. Rocco; Università di Bari), Zenodo 2019, 10.5281/zenodo.3575485; the files are licensed CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (non-commercial use). The summary is our own: language, symbols, technique and cemetery from the EDB fields; the assignment of cemeteries to roads, month of burial, age, offices and formulae from the Latin and Greek texts of the inscriptions (edb/parse.py, edb/calc.py, edb/greek.py, edb/dup.py). On the seasons of death: B. D. Shaw, Seasons of Death: Aspects of Mortality in Imperial Rome, Journal of Roman Studies 86 (1996).
                                • Rome among the inscriptions of the empire. V. Kaše, P. Heřmánková, A. Sobotková: LIST – Latin Inscriptions in Space and Time, v1.2, Zenodo 2024, 10.5281/zenodo.10473706 (CC BY 4.0); its sources are the Epigraphik-Datenbank Clauss/Slaby (EDCS) and the Epigraphic Database Heidelberg (EDH). The assignment to cities is from LIST (based on J. W. Hanson’s list of cities). The summary is our own: text cleaning, formulae, legal status, soldiers and age from the texts of the inscriptions (list/calc.py, list/stats.py, list/fin.py).
                                • Amphora inscriptions. CEIPAC (Universitat de Barcelona, J. Remesal Rodríguez) – Roman Open Data, the open database and SPARQL endpoint of the EPNet project (ERC): romanopendata.eu; queried on 12 November 2026. J. Remesal Rodríguez – G. Rull Fort: Roman Open Data. CEIPAC’s Amphora Epigraphy Database (2021). The summary is our own: the amphorae found in Rome, the district name and year of the δ inscriptions, the pottery of the stamps, the weight in the γ line (amph/base.py, amph/delta.py, amph/calc.py).
                                • Coin hoards. Coin Hoards of the Roman Empire (CHRE), Ashmolean Museum and Oxford Roman Economy Project, University of Oxford: chre.ashmus.ox.ac.uk; CSV download on 12 November 2026; licence: CC BY-NC-SA (non-commercial use). The summary is our own: closing of the hoards in 25-year spans, the hoards found within 10 kilometres of Rome read one by one, material and mint of the coins of the Italian hoards (chre/calc.py). The dates of the events follow the standard historical chronology.
                                • The measured flow of the Anio Novus. D. Keenan-Jones, D. Motta, M. H. Garcia, B. W. Fouke: Travertine-based estimates of the amount of water supplied by ancient Rome's Anio Novus aqueduct, Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 3 (2015) 1–10; D. Motta et al.: Hydraulic evaluation of the design and operation of ancient Rome's Anio Novus aqueduct, Archaeometry 59 (2017) 1150–1174; D. Keenan-Jones et al.: Travertine crystal growth ripples record the hydraulic history of ancient Rome's Anio Novus aqueduct, Scientific Reports 12 (2022) 1239 (CC BY 4.0). The site-by-site values come from Supplementary Table S3 of the 2022 article; for the 2015 and 2017 studies the figures follow the abstract and the authors' own later citations.
                                • The origins of the Romans: ancient DNA and isotopes. M. L. Antonio, Z. Gao, H. M. Moots et al.: Ancient Rome: A genetic crossroads of Europe and the Mediterranean, Science 366 (2019) 708–714 (counts from the text of the article; own summary). K. Killgrove, J. Montgomery: All Roads Lead to Rome, PLOS ONE 11(2) (2016) e0147585 (CC BY 4.0): measurements of the 105 individuals from Tables 1–2, the four non-local individuals according to the authors' statistical test.
                                • Shipwrecks and lead pollution. J. Strauss, A. I. Wilson, M. Flohr: OxREP Shipwrecks Database, version 2.1, Oxford Roman Economy Project 2017 (oxrep.web.ox.ac.uk); used with the consent of the OxREP directors, A. I. Wilson and A. Bowman (e-mails, 25 November 2026: academic re-use with acknowledgement of the source); the map shows own aggregates. For reading the curve: A. Wilson: Developments in Mediterranean shipping and maritime trade from the Hellenistic period to AD 1000, in: D. Robinson, A. Wilson (eds): Maritime Archaeology and Ancient Trade in the Mediterranean, Oxford 2011, 33–60. Lead: J. R. McConnell, A. I. Wilson, A. Stohl, M. M. Arienzo, N. J. Chellman, S. Eckhardt, E. M. Thompson, A. M. Pollard, J. P. Steffensen, PNAS 115 (2018) 5726–5731.
                                • Coin hoards of the Republic. K. Lockyear: Coin Hoards of the Roman Republic Online, American Numismatic Society (numismatics.org/chrr), Open Database License (ODbL 1.0); the full list of hoards was downloaded, the calculations are our own.
                                • Disasters in Rome. Fires: H. V. Canter: Conflagrations in Ancient Rome, Classical Journal 27 (1932) 270–288 (public domain; LacusCurtius). Floods: G. S. Aldrete: Floods of the Tiber in Ancient Rome, Baltimore 2007, list of floods from the ancient authors. Earthquakes: E. Guidoboni et al.: CFTI5Med, Catalogo dei Forti Terremoti in Italia (461 a.C.–1997) e nell’area Mediterranea (760 a.C.–1500), Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia 2018, doi:10.6092/ingv.it-cfti5, CC BY 4.0.
                                • Prices and wages in 301. Edictum Diocletiani de pretiis rerum venalium (AD 301). Edition and numbering: S. Lauffer: Diokletians Preisedikt, Berlin 1971; items read after A. Kropff: An English translation of the Edict on Maximum Prices, also known as the Price Edict of Diocletian, version 2.1, 2016 (after E. R. Graser 1940, Lauffer 1971, Crawford–Reynolds 1979 and Salway 2010). Conversion of measures: Lauffer 1971, 54–55. On the effect of the edict: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 7.6–7. The selection, the item names and the calculations are our own.
                                • Travel time and transport cost. W. Scheidel – E. Meeks: ORBIS: The Stanford Geospatial Network Model of the Roman World, Stanford University (orbis.stanford.edu); description of the model: W. Scheidel: Orbis: the Stanford geospatial network model of the Roman world, Princeton/Stanford Working Papers in Classics, 2015. Six queries of the model with Rome as centre (12 November 2026); the results for 29 selected cities are shown.
                                • The diet of the Romans: carbon and nitrogen isotopes. F. De Angelis et al., Food at the heart of the Empire: dietary reconstruction for Imperial Rome inhabitants, Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 12 (2020) 244 (Tables 2 and 4); S. Varano et al., The edge of the Empire: diet characterization of medieval Rome through stable isotope analysis, ibid. 12 (2020) 196 (Tables 1 and 3). Both CC BY 4.0. The chart is my own drawing from the published means.
                                • Office-holders of the Republic. Digital Prosopography of the Roman Republic (DPRR), King’s College London, romanrepublic.ac.uk; RDF version and SPARQL endpoint: John Bradley (CC BY-NC 4.0). Downloaded on 12 November 2026; the figures on the card are own aggregates.
                                • Building activity over time. The map’s own data: the “cronologia di impianto/fondazione” entries of the SITAR excavation units (SITAR – Sistema Informativo Territoriale Archeologico di Roma, archeositarproject.it), and the construction dates of the map’s features. Units dated to a period are distributed by the aoristic method (J. H. Ratcliffe, “Aoristic analysis: the spatial interpretation of unspecific temporal events”, International Journal of Geographical Information Science 14 (2000) 669–679).
                                • Feeding Rome. Josephus, Jewish War 2.383, 2.386; Epitome de Caesaribus 1.6; Res gestae 15; Tacitus, Annals 1.7; Suetonius, Claudius 18–19; Gaius, Institutes 1.32c; Digest 50.5.3; Historia Augusta, Severus 18.3, 23.2, Aurelian 35.2, 47.1, 48.1–4. P. Garnsey – D. Rathbone, “The Background to the Grain Law of Gaius Gracchus”, Journal of Roman Studies 75 (1985) 20–25. Monte Testaccio: H. Dressel, Ricerche sul Monte Testaccio, Rome 1878; E. Rodríguez Almeida, Il Monte Testaccio: ambiente, storia, materiali, Rome 1984; J. M. Blázquez Martínez – J.                                 • Course of the walks. The streets of OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL): the excavated streets of the Forum and the Palatine tagged with their ancient names (Via Sacra, Via Nova, Clivus Capitolinus, Vicus Tuscus, etc.), and present-day streets that, according to the topographical literature, preserve the line of an ancient street (for example the Via del Corso that of the Via Lata, the Via Urbana that of the Vicus Patricius); the classification of the latter is the map author’s own and has not been checked street by street. In addition, the road network of the map.
                                • Present-day relief. Regione Lazio, Digital Terrain Model (DTM) – passo 5 m – v. 2002/2003 (from the photogrammetric points of the Carta Tecnica Regionale Numerica 1:5000), CC BY 4.0, Geoportale Regione Lazio. It shows the present-day surface: in the valleys the ancient ground level lies 5–15 m deeper, and the modern roads, embankments and fills are also visible in it.

                                Overviews

                                • List of monuments of the Roman Forum; Seindal: Basilica Iulia; L. Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992); A. Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2010); F. Coarelli, Rome and Environs.
                                Ground plan made for study purposes. The outlines follow the survey of the ruins visible today (OpenStreetMap), so they mostly show the final, imperial-period state; the monuments of the Forum burned down and were rebuilt several times.
